newsitem.title: USA: Pixar shares jump on better-than-expected profits.
newsitem.headline: Pixar shares jump on better-than-expected profits.

text.p: Stock in computer animation company Pixar Inc. rose sharply Friday after the company reported second-quarter revenues and earnings that were more than double Wall Street expectations.

The Richmond, Calif.-based company said late Thursday its revenues jumped to $14.4 million in the quarter from $6.9 million a year ago and earned 19 cents a share compared with 10 cents a share in the year-ago period.
The results blew past analysts' average forecast of 9 cents a share, according to figures compiled by First Call, and drove the stock price up $1.50 to $17.375 on Nasdaq on Friday.

Pixar, which creates computer-generated animated feature films, scored a big hit in October 1995 with its first film, Walt Disney Co.'s "Toy Story," which took in $350 million worldwide at the box office.
The results prompted Keith Benjamin, an analyst for Robertson Stephens and Co., to raise his estimate for the company's 1997 yearly earnings to 29 cents a share from 26 cents a share.

"These revenues and earnings are still from the first movie," Benjamin said. "This quarter gave the last bit of evidence that both Disney and Pixar were able to generate lots of revenues" from home video sources and merchandising.
He described the company as a "compelling long-term investment," and hinged his positive outlook on new products not yet announced and "It's a Bugs Life," a new film due out in late 1998.
Benjamin also said he sees the stock's price holding near $20 a share before accelerating as the release of "Bugs" approaches. Earnings could exceed $1 per share by 1999.

Revenues during future quarters may trail off due to the lack of significant new products. But other projects, such as a planned direct-to-video sequel to "Toy Story," will keep the market primed for the next burst of revenues, Benjamin said.
Harold Vogel, an analyst at Cowen and Co., says the company is positioning itself to better take advantage of toy merchandising and other cross-marketing opportunities from the film.
The recent addition of Jill Barad, chief executive of toymaker Mattel Corp., to Pixar's board, should help in that effort, Vogel said.
"It's obvious that they want to get a head start on the toy product line tie-ins with the next release," Vogel said.
